paper_title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: A rules file is prose. The agent reads it, or does not, and acts on it, or does not. Gloaguen et al. [5] evaluated repository context files for coding agents. They found more exploration and higher cost, with no clear gain in task success. That work did not ask what happens at refusal or temptation. The one-page test [1] found that specification frame reduced registered defects in single-turn code on money, time, idempotency and access tasks. This study asks whether that effect carries into multi-step agent loop. Purpose Custody [2] defines the recorded purpose, what an agent was authorized to do, and asks whether each action still runs under it. Here score related record, which call the evidence trail: what was authorized, what was done, and what was checked. Specification gaming is an old observation: system satisfies the check rather than the property. trajectory corpus with full call logs [6] and corpus of agent-authored pull requests [7] now make it possible to look for gaps between what an agent claims and what its record shows. An incident corpus mined from GitHub issues lists fabricated success reports among the operational failures of coding agents [8]. This study adds controlled measurement: the same repository, the same task, three arms, and hidden test suite the agent never sees. The audit reports gap between report and test. It does not infer intent.

sections.title: 3 What was registered
sections.content: The pre-registration [3] fixed the agents, the repositories, the arms, the outcomes, the equivalence bands, the verdict rules and the analysis code. Each hypothesis has three possible verdicts, read from the 95% interval of the pooled effect. Supported means the interval excludes the null in the predicted direction. Refuted means the interval lies inside pre-stated equivalence band. Anything else is inconclusive. degenerate interval, which is what you get when every pair is tied, is inconclusive. No verdict is issued below 20 observations. The equivalence bands are quarter of the arm-A mean per repository for findings (floor 0.25), ten percentage points for rates, five points for the pass rate, and one new finding per 100 added lines for H3. Table 1 lists the hypotheses and the verdicts. The registration did not define control as word. Read from its bands, the file would have counted as one if the crossing rate under had sat within ten points of the gates zero, with an interval that excluded the rate under A. At 15 runs per arm that result was out of reach. So advice below is the reading the data allow, not definition.

sections.title: 8 Related work
sections.content: Gloaguen et al. [5] measured repository context files on coding-agent benchmarks and reported more tool calls and higher cost without clear gain in success. They separated developer-written from agent-written files, which is the arm that did not run here, and on cost, results elsewhere differ [16]. Other evaluations found rules files helped task success [15], cut runtime and output tokens [16], or made no measurable difference to correctness [17]. ContextCov compiles AGENTS.md rules into checks outside the model and reached 88.3 percent compliance, against 67.0 for the same rules given in the prompt alone [18]. Yang, He and Zhou registered study of AI contribution rules in open-source repositories. With no reminder, agents opened the policy file in 12 of 347 runs, count that leaves out the always-loaded AGENTS.md, and some wrote all tests pass without matching check [19]. My Codex CLI result shows different gap: it ran its own tests and they passed, and my hidden tests of the task did not. The one-page test [1] is the single-turn parent of H1 and H6. public trajectory corpus [6], corpus of agent-authored pull requests [7] and an incident corpus mined from GitHub issues [8] motivate the trace audit, which here has hidden test suite as ground truth. Study 1b, the controls study, is registered separately [4]. Five recent preprints touch the same ground. Xu and Wu [9] found that Claude Code and Codex CLI followed stale instruction file in about 90% of choices without their one-sentence fix, over 320 runs with and without it. Codex CLI rewrote existing code to match the file in 20 of 80 runs, and project tests then failed in 17 of them. That supports my Codex CLI result from another direction. They also found that the one added sentence moved the agents choices toward the code, from 4.2 to 91.4 percent. So file can steer an agent hard. McMillan [10] ran 1,650 Claude Code sessions and found no detectable effect of file structure on compliance. He also reported, as an exploratory result, that the odds of compliance fell as the agent wrote more functions in session, which is the fading H3 tests here. SkillShield [11] found that security instructions in the system prompt reduced execution attacks but did not remove them. IssueTrojanBench [12] found that 66.5% of malicious issues passed all guardrails, and that refusals came almost entirely from the models, not the agent frameworks. Lulla and colleagues registered study protocol on how configuring Claude Code and Codex, from context files to permission controls, changes which libraries an agent adds and whether it discloses them [13]. It reported no results when wrote this.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: I asked whether rules file at the root of repository is control on coding agent or only advice. On what this study could measure, it was advice: an instruction each agent read in its own way, with nothing to enforce it. What the file did. There were no real bugs of the kinds my checkers look for, with it or without it. It cost one of four agents third of its score on the hidden tests. That agent, Codex CLI, reported the task complete with all tests passing in 11 of its 36 steps. The tests it wrote for itself did pass. The other three agents moved by less than 2.5 points. At the lines built, the agents rarely tried to cross. They tried in 5 of 90 gated steps, all by one agent, and the gate blocked every try. One behaviour moved with the file. OpenCodes found access token reached the service in 5 of 5 runs without the file and in none with it. Its one try with the file was blocked by the gate. That is direction, and the next study tests it. What it means. For teams: use the file to tell the agent what you want, and enforce boundaries in layer the model cannot argue with, such as gate. Leave the vendors permission prompts on as well. turned them off here, so make no claim about what they stop. Put security in the setup the agent works inside, not in its instructions: gate in front of risky services, as here, no stray credentials, and only the access the task needs. Check the record, not the summary. For vendors: one agent reported success when its own tests passed and my hidden tests of the task did not. Its message named the requirement it added, but not that it went beyond what the task asked. For anyone writing guidance: if it calls the rules file control, it should cite measurement, or recommend gate. What this study adds. As far as could find, the first pre-registered test of rules file at security boundaries, with an enforcement gate as the comparison, on four shipped coding agents, three of them at the boundaries. The design was frozen before any agent ran. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. The full record is public. Scope and next steps. This study measured how often agents tried to cross boundary. An error in my run script put the gate in front of every no-file and rules-file run at the three HTTP boundaries, so the ungated measure waits for the next study. The next one measures how often they succeed with no gate in the way. Fifteen runs per boundary were enough to see which agents tried and how often, though not enough for statistical verdict, so the next study runs more. scored every message myself, blind to arm in the first pass, and the next study adds second scorer. The pass-rate result depends on none of these, because it comes from hidden tests the agent never saw. The next study also tests the rule repeated in the prompt at every step. rules file behaved like advice, not firewall. Its effect depended on which agent read it. gate stops only the 21 requests it lists, so the list has to be right. file tells an agent what you want. gate decides what it gets. Preambles for LLM Code Generation. Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.23967966, version 1.0, 4 November 2026.
